introduction-the-architects-compass.core: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of design principles and review questions across six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. It's a structured way to find risks and trade-offs in a workload, not a certification or checklist to pass.

first_principles.problem: Architecture reviews are ad hoc and miss whole categories of risk.
truths: Risks should be prioritised and tracked.

analogy.title: A compass with six directions
analogy.story: It doesn't tell you the route, but it stops you heading the wrong way.
analogy.breaks: A compass has fixed directions; pillar priorities vary by business.

example.title: A review outcome
flow: Reliability: no tested restore → high risk
Security: root user without MFA → high risk

check.a: No, it's a review framework for identifying and prioritising risks and improvements.

pillar-1-operational-excellence.core: Operational excellence is about running and improving workloads: operations as code, small frequent reversible changes, observability, runbooks and game days, and learning from failures through post-incident reviews. The goal is reliable delivery of business value with fast feedback.

first_principles.problem: Deploys are big, manual and scary, and incidents repeat because lessons aren't captured.
truths: Small changes are easier to roll back.

analogy.title: A Formula 1 pit crew
analogy.story: Rehearsed procedures, telemetry on everything and debriefs after every race.
analogy.breaks: Pit stops are identical each time; incidents vary, so runbooks need judgement too.

check.q: Why do small, frequent changes improve operations?
check.a: Each change carries less risk, is easier to diagnose and quicker to roll back.

pillar-2-security.core: The security pillar covers a strong identity foundation (least privilege, centralised identity), traceability (logging and monitoring), security at every layer, protecting data in transit and at rest, automating security controls and preparing for incidents. Security is designed in, not bolted on.

first_principles.problem: Security reviews happen at the end and block launches with long lists of findings.

analogy.title: Building security into a house's design
analogy.story: Locks, alarms and fire exits planned in the blueprint, not added after move-in.
analogy.breaks: Houses face few threats; cloud workloads face constant automated attacks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Security review passes on day one.

check.q: Name two design principles of the security pillar.
check.a: Implement a strong identity foundation and enable traceability (also automate security, protect data, prepare for events).

pillar-3-reliability.core: Reliability means a workload performs its function correctly and consistently. Principles: automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, and manage change through automation. Key practices are multi-AZ design, service quotas management, backups with tested restores and fault isolation.

first_principles.problem: A system survives normal days but collapses during an AZ failure or traffic surge.
truths: Many small resources fail more gracefully than one big one.

analogy.title: A bridge designed with redundant supports
analogy.story: If one support fails, others carry the load, and engineers load-test it before opening.
analogy.breaks: Bridges don't change daily; software changes are a leading cause of failure.

example.title: Restore test
flow: Restore prod DB snapshot to isolated account

check.q: What's the difference between RTO and RPO?
check.a: RTO is how quickly you must recover; RPO is how much data loss (time) is acceptable.

pillar-4-performance-efficiency.core: Performance efficiency means using resources efficiently as demand changes: choose the right resource types (instance families, managed services, databases), go global in minutes, use serverless where it fits, experiment often and practise mechanical sympathy (use technology aligned with how it works best).

first_principles.problem: A team runs analytics on an OLTP database and wonders why it's slow and expensive.
truths: The cloud lets you try options cheaply.

analogy.title: Using the right vehicle for each delivery
analogy.story: Motorbikes for city documents, lorries for furniture, planes for overseas.
analogy.breaks: Vehicles are bought; cloud resources can be swapped in minutes, so re-evaluate often.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each workload on the right engine.

check.a: Using technologies in ways that align with how they work best, e.g. access patterns suited to the database.

pillar-5-cost-optimization.core: Cost optimisation means delivering business value at the lowest price point: practise cloud financial management, adopt a consumption model (pay only for what you use), measure efficiency (cost per transaction), stop spending on undifferentiated heavy lifting (managed services) and analyse and attribute expenditure.

first_principles.problem: Dev environments run 24/7 and production is sized for peak all year.
truths: Managed services trade price for toil.

analogy.title: Paying for electricity
analogy.story: Turn off lights in empty rooms, use efficient appliances and get a cheaper tariff for steady use.
analogy.breaks: Electricity has one price; cloud has hundreds of pricing dimensions.

check.a: It shows efficiency independent of growth: total cost can rise while unit cost falls.

pillar-6-sustainability.core: The sustainability pillar minimises environmental impact: understand your impact (Customer Carbon Footprint Tool), maximise utilisation, use efficient hardware (Graviton, latest generations), use managed services, reduce data stored and moved, and choose regions with cleaner energy where possible.

first_principles.problem: Idle, oversized infrastructure wastes energy as well as money.
truths: Newer hardware does more per watt.
Unused data still consumes storage energy.

analogy.title: Car-sharing and efficient engines
analogy.story: Fewer cars running full, with efficient engines, cut emissions.
analogy.breaks: Cars emit directly; cloud emissions depend on the grid mix behind each region.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Lower carbon and lower cost together.

check.q: Name two sustainability practices on AWS.
check.a: Use efficient hardware like Graviton and maximise utilisation through autoscaling or serverless (also reduce stored data).
